none.label: Local only — nothing is deployed anywhere; `make verify` is the end of the road

aws.label: AWS — one ECS service per app deployed blue/green behind its own load balancer, RDS Postgres, Cognito and S3 + CloudFront, provisioned by OpenTofu and deployed by the trunk pipeline

azure.label: Azure — one Container App per app deployed by revision behind the environment's own ingress and managed certificate, PostgreSQL Flexible Server, Entra ID and Static Web Apps, provisioned by OpenTofu and deployed by the trunk pipeline

existing.label: Existing — this project deploys to infrastructure it does not own: whatever runs it is described in `docs/deployment.md` and provisioned by nobody here; `make verify` is the gate and nothing is deployed by the factory

write-model.description: How a service decides and records a write — which is to say where this product keeps its truth. Both answers raise the same typed events the model names; what differs is whether the log is the truth or a consequence of it. Only one direction is cheap: a log folds down into tables whenever you decide it should, so a service can stop being event-sourced, but state cannot be turned back into history it never recorded. Asked per service, and the one answer about a service that cannot be walked back once it holds data

events.label: Event-sourced — the log is the truth and state is a fold of it. Rung 4: nothing is lost, a read model nobody thought of is a replay away, and the cost of a slice stays flat as the system grows. For a service that owns its truth, whose behaviour is business operations rather than field updates, and whose past is worth something

state.label: State-stored — the service keeps current state, and its events are the model's contracts, raised after each write and never replayed. Rung 2: the cheaper start, for a service that is not the owner of what it holds, or whose past nobody will ask about

persistence.description: How this service keeps its data. Every answer is one store behind one port, and the in-memory adapter ships with all of them, so `make verify` needs no Docker whichever store is chosen

memory.label: In-memory — zero infrastructure, loses all truth on restart. The adapter the port's contract runs against in `make verify`

sqlite.label: SQLite — a real append-only log in one file, no container. Serialised writes, so it cannot prove concurrent behaviour

postgres.label: Postgres — append-only table, unique (stream, version) as the concurrency control

http.prompt: Inbound HTTP (inferred from the backend, never asked)
http.description: What accepts inbound HTTP. One transport per backend, the ecosystem's own, or none for a library or worker

none.label: None — library or worker only, no inbound HTTP

auth.description: Who authenticates the people who run the product — staff, operators, support. Every provider on this axis is an OIDC issuer and OIDC is what the adapters speak, so the protocol is the one thing every answer has in common — which is why the axis is named for the role and not for it

keycloak.label: Keycloak — self-hosted OIDC, container and group mapping scaffolded (the flow itself is NOT implemented)

cognito.label: Cognito — a user pool with the internal groups, a hosted login and a confidential client, provisioned in AWS; Keycloak runs locally as the stand-in, with the same groups and OIDC_* keys (the flow itself is NOT implemented)

entra.label: Entra ID — an app registration with the internal groups and a confidential client, provisioned in the subscription's own workforce tenant; Keycloak runs locally as the stand-in, with the same groups and OIDC_* keys (the flow itself is NOT implemented)

auth0.label: Auth0 — an application, an API and the internal roles, provisioned through Auth0's own Management API rather than by the cloud, with a post-login action putting the roles in a namespaced claim; Keycloak runs locally as the stand-in, with the same groups and OIDC_* keys (the flow itself is NOT implemented)

users.description: Who authenticates the people the product is for — accounts anyone on the internet can create, with sign-up, verification, password reset and a login the browser app owns. Never the internal directory: a separate realm or tenant, even on the same vendor. Every answer is an OIDC issuer, so a service validates an external token the way it validates an internal one, against a different issuer

keycloak.label: Keycloak — an external realm beside the internal one in the same container, self-registration and password reset on, a public PKCE client for the browser app; the browser login is real, and a service's token validation is the framework's where one owns startup and NOT implemented where none does

cognito.label: Cognito — a second user pool for external users with self-registration and a public PKCE client, provisioned in AWS; Keycloak's external realm runs locally as the stand-in, and the browser login is real

auth0.label: Auth0 — a database connection with self-registration and password reset, and a public PKCE client for the browser app, provisioned through Auth0's own Management API rather than by the cloud; Keycloak's external realm is the local stand-in, and the browser login is real

standard.label: Standard — the walking skeleton, the executable test and the CD gate, and no model of the workflow behind them. Features are specified one at a time and a service keeps current state: the honest answer where the system is not the owner of its truth, its behaviour is field updates rather than business operations, and nobody will ask what happened last month

event-modelling.label: Event Modeling — everything above, plus the workflow modelled before it is built and delivered one stamped slice at a time, every event a named business fact. Where truth lives is a separate question, asked per service: the model is the same on either rung, and what changes is the write model
